exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with frothy, yellow discharge and itching. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — Recognise trichomoniasis; perform wet mount and treat with metronidazole.
A post‑menopausal patient reports burning and spotting; pH is 5.5. How does this guide management? — Suggest atrophic vaginitis; start topical estrogen.

A patient with HIV has thick white discharge and no itching. Which organism is likely and why avoid fluconazole in severe liver disease? — Candida; fluconazole is hepatotoxic, consider topical azoles.

You see a friable, red vaginal lesion in a 45‑year‑old woman. What is the differential and immediate action? — Consider HPV lesion vs. ulcerative STI; obtain biopsy and test for HSV, treat accordingly.
A woman with bacterial vaginosis does not improve after oral metronidazole. What are alternative strategies? — Use vaginal metronidazole gel or clindamycin; assess adherence and reinfection.
During a pelvic exam you note a yellowish discharge but pH 4.0. How do you interpret this? — Normal pH argues against bacterial vaginosis; likely candidiasis or physiologic discharge.
A pregnant woman presents with vaginal itching and white curdy discharge. What is safe treatment? — Topical clotrimazole; avoid systemic azoles.
A patient reports heavy vaginal bleeding after intercourse. What red flag does this represent? — Possible cervical or vaginal malignancy; arrange urgent referral and biopsy.
ai.title: Disorders of the Vagina
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Vaginal disorders range from infections to neoplasia and structural problems. In low‑resource settings common causes include bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, trichomoniasis, and HPV‑related lesions. Clinical reasoning focuses on pattern recognition, targeted testing and pragmatic management.

b: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by microscopy, pH testing and simple cultures when available.
sections.p: Any pathological change affecting the vaginal mucosa, secretions or flora, presenting with discharge, itching, pain or bleeding.

t.b: Is the environment acidic (≤4.5) or raised? A pH >4.5 suggests bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis or atrophic vaginitis.
What organisms or clue cells are present? Clue cells indicate bacterial vaginosis; hyphae/pseudohyphae indicate candidiasis; motile trophozoites indicate trichomoniasis.
Which bacteria are predominant? Guides targeted antibiotics for gonorrhoea or chlamydia.
What lesions are seen? Identifies ulcerative, papular or neoplastic lesions needing biopsy.

b: Mild: discharge only, no erythema.
Moderate: discharge plus erythema, itching or mild pain.
Severe: ulceration, extensive bleeding, or suspicion of neoplasia.
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden and extent of mucosal involvement.

b: Bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella vaginalis overgrowth).
Candida albicans infection (often after antibiotics or diabetes).
Trichomonas vaginalis (sexually transmitted, common in HIV‑positive women).
Sexually transmitted infections: gonorrhoea, chlamydia.
Atrophic vaginitis (post‑menopausal, low estrogen).
HPV‑related intraepithelial neoplasia (precursor to cancer).
Schistosoma haematobium deposition (rare, causes granulomas).
sections.p: In East African low‑resource hospitals the most frequent aetiologies are:

b: Thin, fishy smelling discharge → bacterial vaginosis.
Thick, cottage‑cheese discharge → candidiasis.
Frothy, yellow‑green discharge with itching → trichomoniasis.
Painful ulcer or mass → consider HPV lesion or ulcerative STI.
sections.p: Patients may report abnormal discharge, pruritus, burning, dyspareunia, or spotting. Systemic signs are uncommon unless there is a co‑existing STI or severe infection.

b: Speculum exam, pH strip, wet mount are low‑cost and high yield.
sections.p: Use bedside tools first; send specimens only when they will change management.

t.a: Vaginal swab for rapid antigen test (if available)
t.b: Does the patient have gonorrhoea or chlamydia? Positive result directs appropriate antibiotics.
Is the lesion neoplastic? Histology confirms intraepithelial neoplasia or carcinoma.
Is the patient immunocompromised? Positive result influences choice of antifungal and STI management.

b: Severe pain, fever, or foul‑smelling discharge → possible pelvic inflammatory disease.
Persistent ulceration or mass → possible invasive cancer.
Heavy bleeding unresponsive to local measures → consider coagulopathy or malignancy.
sections.p: Identify patients who need urgent referral or inpatient care.

b: Atrophic vaginitis: topical estrogen cream – restores mucosal integrity; avoid systemic estrogen in estrogen‑dependent cancers.
HPV lesions: cryotherapy or topical imiquimod – destroys dysplastic cells; avoid destructive surgery in pregnancy.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve symptoms and prevent recurrence.

b: Review at 2 weeks to confirm symptom resolution.
Educate on condom use, genital hygiene, and avoidance of douching.
Vaccinate eligible women against HPV.
Screen HIV‑positive women regularly for opportunistic vaginal infections.
sections.p: Re‑evaluate symptoms after treatment and counsel on risk reduction.

b: Urinary tract infection – dysuria without discharge; urine dipstick helps.
Dermatitis of vulva – external erythema, often allergic; no vaginal discharge.
Cervical ectropion – bleeding on contact, not discharge; speculum exam distinguishes.
Normal pH does not exclude candidiasis.
Negative wet mount may miss low‑level Trichomonas; consider PCR if available.
Gram stain may show mixed flora; clinical correlation essential.

whenToSeekHelp: High fever, severe pelvic pain, or foul‑smelling discharge
Visible ulcer or mass suspicious for cancer
